fact: The federal carpet and rug flammability standard, 16 CFR 1630, lights a methenamine tablet on each of eight 9-by-9-inch samples held flat under a steel plate with an 8-inch hole; a sample passes if its char stops more than 1 inch short of the hole's edge, and at least seven of the eight must pass.
quote: (a) Summary of test method. This method involves the exposure of each of eight conditioned, replicate specimens of a given carpet or rug to a standard igniting source in a draft-protected environment, and measurement of the proximity of the charred portion to the edge of the hole in the prescribed flattening frame. (b) Test criterion. A specimen passes the test if the charred portion does not extend to within 2.54 cm. (1.0 in.) of the edge of the hole in the flattening frame at any point. (c) Acceptance criterion. At least seven of the eight specimens shall meet the test criterion in order to conform with this Standard. … (2) Flattening frame. A steel plate, 22.86 × 22.86 cm. (9 × 9 in.), … with a 20.32 cm. (8 in.) diameter hole in its center is required to hold the carpet or rug flat during the course of the test. … (3) Standard igniting source. A methenamine tablet, flat, with a nominal heat of combustion value of 7180 calories/gram, a mass of 150 mg ±5 mg and a nominal diameter of 6mm.
source_label: eCFR, 16 CFR Part 1630, Standard for the Surface Flammability of Carpets and Rugs (FF 1-70), §§ 1630.3 and 1630.4(a)
notes: Read in full through the eCFR versioner API (title 16, part 1630, as of 2026-09-01) on 2026-09-25; the human eCFR page redirects automated fetches. The regulation covers carpets and rugs and does not name artificial turf; ASTM D2859 is the trade's near-copy of this method (see is-artificial-turf-flammable.astm-d2859-limits).

fact: ASTM describes D2859 as similar but not identical to the federal carpet tests, run in the lab on a sample lying flat with no underlay specified, able to identify floor coverings that can be rated flame-resistant under those controlled conditions, and not by itself enough to judge fire hazard under actual fire conditions.
quote: 1.1.2 This test method is similar but not identical to the test methods contained in 16 CFR 1630 and CFR 1631 and issued by CPSC. If compliance with one of the CPSC test methods is required, this test method does not ensure regulatory compliance. … 1.4 This standard is used to measure and describe the response of materials, products, or assemblies to heat and flame under controlled conditions, but does not by itself incorporate all factors required for fire hazard or fire risk assessment of the materials, products, or assemblies under actual fire conditions. … 5.1 This test method provides a procedure for identification of those finished textile floor covering materials that can be rated as flame-resistant under specific controlled laboratory conditions. 5.2 This test method does not specify the use of an underlay material. … 5.3 In this test, results are observed with the specimens in a horizontal plane. Different results are possible if the same material is tested or used in any other plane.
source_label: ASTM D2859-16(2021), Standard Test Method for Ignition Characteristics of Finished Textile Floor Covering Materials: Scope 1.1.2 and 1.4, Significance and Use 5.1 to 5.3
notes: Read on ASTM's store page (the standard's published scope and significance) on 2026-09-25. D2859-16(2021) is the active version. The full method is sold by ASTM; the federal method it mirrors is quoted in is-artificial-turf-flammable.cfr-1630-pill-test.

fact: ASTM E648, the radiant-panel test, measures the critical radiant flux at which flame spreading across a horizontally mounted floor covering goes out; ASTM says it was developed to simulate fires in building corridors and exitways and is not intended for routine use in judging flame spread elsewhere.
quote: 1.1 This fire-test-response standard covers a procedure for measuring the critical radiant flux of horizontally mounted floor-covering systems exposed to a flaming ignition source in a graded radiant heat energy environment in a test chamber. … 1.2 This fire-test-response standard measures the critical radiant flux at flame-out. It provides a basis for estimating one aspect of fire exposure behavior for floor-covering systems. … The standard was developed to simulate an important fire exposure component of fires that develop in corridors or exitways of buildings and is not intended for routine use in estimating flame spread behavior of floor covering in building areas other than corridors or exitways.
source_label: ASTM E648-25a, Standard Test Method for Critical Radiant Flux of Floor-Covering Systems Using a Radiant Heat Energy Source: Scope 1.1 and 1.2
notes: Read on ASTM's store page on 2026-09-25; E648-25a is listed as the active version. Result classes for the test are set by building and life-safety codes, not quoted here.

quote: Flammability Passed - D-2859 … TESTING DATA FIRE ASTM E108, ASTM D2859, ASTM E648
source_label: SYNLawn, SYNAugustine 847 product specifications (SKU S847B), page 2, dated December 10, 2025
notes: Read with pdftotext on 2026-09-25. Cited as an example of how a sheet presents fire tests, not as a recommendation; the same sheet is cited for its other test methods in turf-spec-sheet-for-colorado.synlawn-847-test-methods.

fact: The Colorado State Forest Service calls grasses perhaps the most pervasive surface fuel in Colorado: they catch fire easily, spread fire rapidly and burn out quickly, and grass fuels can readily ignite structures directly next to them.
quote: Grasses are perhaps the most pervasive and abundant surface fuel in Colorado. When available to burn, grasses can catch fire easily, and grass fires often spread rapidly. They also burn out quickly and do not release as much energy as fires in larger fuel types, like trees. Nonetheless, grass fuels can readily ignite structures that are directly adjacent to them.
source_label: Colorado State Forest Service, The Home Ignition Zone: A guide to preparing your home for wildfire and creating defensible space (2021), Fuel types: Grasses
notes: Read with curl and pdftotext on 2026-09-25. The PDF's text layer drops the 'fi' ligature ('fre'); the quote restores the printed word 'fire'.

fact: The Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety says the 5 feet around a home is where embers, flames and radiant heat reach it, and that its laboratory testing and post-fire investigations consistently show removing all combustible materials from those 5 feet is the most effective defensible-space action a homeowner can take.
quote: Research from the Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety (IBHS) shows that the 5-foot area immediately surrounding a home—known as the Noncombustible Zone 0, Home Ignition Zone (HIZ), or ember-resistant zone—is one of the most important areas for reducing wildfire risk . This is where embers, flames, and radiant heat associated with wildfire reach the home. … Laboratory testing and post-fire investigations have consistently shown that removing all combustible materials from this 5-foot zone is the most effective defensible space action homeowners can take to reduce the risk of home ignition .
source_label: Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety, Noncombustible Zone 0: Minimizing Pathways to Home Ignition
notes: Read with curl on 2026-09-25. The spaces before the periods are the page's (link markup). The page does not name artificial turf; the institute's designation standard does (is-artificial-turf-flammable.ibhs-wph-zone0-turf).

fact: IBHS's Wildfire Prepared Home standard, aimed at wind-driven embers, requires the first 5 feet around a home and its attachments to be noncombustible, measured from the exterior walls and any combustible deck's or overhead structure's outermost posts, with artificial turf, wood and rubber mulch and exposed weed cloth removed to bare mineral soil and gravel, pavers, river rock, decomposed granite and concrete permitted.
quote: Wildfire Prepared Home – Base (Essential) – Provides essential home protection from wind-driven embers by addressing vulnerable building features, vegetation and combustible items on and around the building, reducing pathways for fire to spread to the structure. … The first five feet surrounding the building and its attachments (e.g., patios, decks, stairs, and overhead structures) is the most critical area of defensible space. This zone shall be established and maintained as noncombustible. The 0-5 Foot Noncombustible Zone is measured horizontally from the edge of the building’s exterior walls and, if present, the outermost posts of a combustible deck or overhead structure, extending outward to 5 feet (see Figure 2). … Groundcover – Shall remove all combustible groundcover materials (e.g., wood and rubber mulch, artificial turf, and exposed weed cloth) within 5 feet to bare mineral soil. Note: Noncombustible hardscape materials (e.g., bare dirt, gravel, pavers, river rocks, decomposed granite, steppingstones, and concrete) are permitted.
source_label: Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety, Wildfire Prepared Home Technical Standard (December 2025), Sections 1.1.2 and 2.2.1
notes: Read with pdftotext on 2026-09-25. Bullet glyphs dropped from the quote. A voluntary designation standard, not a code; the page presents it as IBHS's program.

fact: The same IBHS standard lists artificial turf among the combustible items to remove from the walking surface of an attached deck or patio, and requires artificial turf and other combustible groundcover under an elevated deck to be removed to bare mineral soil.
quote: 2.1.5.2 Top of Walking Surfaces … Combustible Items – Combustible items shall be removed, including but not limited to: sheds (including noncombustible sheds), saunas, storage containers, combustible privacy dividers, artificial turf, large area rugs, plastic covers, … 2.1.5.4 Underneath an Elevated Deck – Vegetation and Groundcover - Shall remove all vegetation and combustible groundcover (e.g., grass, artificial turf, weeds, plants, shrubs, bushes, trees, exposed weed cloth, wood and rubber mulch) to bare mineral soil.
source_label: Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety, Wildfire Prepared Home Technical Standard (December 2025), Sections 2.1.5.2 and 2.1.5.4
notes: Read with pdftotext on 2026-09-25. Section 2.1.5 covers attached patios, decks and overhead structures containing any combustible materials. Bullet glyphs dropped.

fact: IBHS's standard defines combustible as materials that can ignite and burn, and noncombustible as material of which no part will ignite and burn when subjected to fire, or any material passing ASTM E136, a vertical tube furnace test at 750°C; it lists ASTM E108 as the fire test for roof coverings, and describes a Red Flag Warning as warm temperatures, very low humidities and strong winds combining to raise fire danger.
quote: Combustible – Materials that can ignite and burn. … Noncombustible – Made from material of which no part will ignite and burn when subjected to fire. Any material passing ASTM E136 shall be considered noncombustible. … Red Flag Warning – A Red Flag Warning is determined by local offices of the National Weather Service (NWS) and is specific to those local areas. A Red Flag Warning means warm temperatures, very low humidities, and strong winds are expected to combine to produce an increased risk of fire danger. … E108 – Standard Test Methods for Fire Tests of Roof Coverings … E136 – Standard Test Method for Behavior of Materials in a Vertical Tube Furnace at 750°C
source_label: Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety, Wildfire Prepared Home Technical Standard (December 2025), Sections 4.3 Definitions and 4.4.1 ASTM referenced standards
notes: Read with pdftotext on 2026-09-25. Bullet glyphs dropped.

fact: IBHS's Wildfire Prepared Home designation program is available in Colorado.
quote: The Wildfire Prepared Home™ designation program empowers homeowners to take science-based, proven steps to meaningfully reduce wildfire risk to their home and property. Now available in AZ, CA, CO, FL, ID, MT, NV, NM, OK, OR, UT, TX, WA, WY !
source_label: Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety, Wildfire Prepared Home (program home page)
notes: Read with curl on 2026-09-25. The standard says to check the site's 'Resources by State' page for current availability; recheck, since the state list changes.

fact: EPA says scrap tires are difficult to ignite, but that once a tire fire starts it is generally very hard to control and put out, water or foam is often futile, and smothering it with dirt or sand is usually the way to extinguish it.
quote: Waste tires are difficult to ignite, but once a tire fire starts, it is generally very hard to control and extinguish. Using water and/or foam to extinguish a tire fire is often futile. Water is best used to keep adjacent, unburned tires from igniting. Smothering a tire fire with dirt or sand is usually the best option for extinguishing fires.
source_label: U.S. EPA, Scrap Tires: Tire Fires (archived web page)
notes: Read with curl on 2026-09-25. EPA's archive of a former Wastes page; it describes scrap tires in piles, not crumb rubber infill in turf, and the page says so. Crumb rubber is ground scrap tire (is-crumb-rubber-safe.epa-qa-how-made).

fact: SB23-166 created Colorado's Wildfire Resiliency Code Board to adopt minimum codes for hardening structures and reducing fire risk in the defensible space around them in the wildland-urban interface, and requires a local government with building- or fire-code authority in that area to adopt a code that meets or exceeds the board's within 3 months of the board adopting it.
quote: The act establishes a wildfire resiliency code board (board) in the division of fire prevention and control (division) within the department of public safety (department) … The board is required to promulgate rules concerning the adoption of codes and standards for the hardening of structures and reducing fire risk in the defensible space surrounding structures in the wildland-urban interface in Colorado … The act requires a governing body with jurisdiction in an area within the wildland-urban interface that has the authority to adopt building codes or fire codes to adopt and enforce a code that meets or exceeds the minimum standards of the codes adopted by the board within 3 months of the date the board adopts its codes.
source_label: SB23-166 bill summary (as enacted), Colorado General Assembly (approved May 12, 2023)
notes: Read 2026-09-25 (the site answers 406 to a bare curl; a browser Accept header reads it). Not legal advice. The board's code is the 2025 Colorado Wildfire Resiliency Code, CWRC Version 1.0, dated June 1, 2025 (cover of Larimer County's recorded copy).

fact: Larimer County's Board of County Commissioners unanimously adopted the 2025 Wildfire Resiliency Code with county amendments on September 22, 2025, effective January 1, 2026.
quote: 2025 Wildfire Resiliency Code - Effective January 1, 2026 The Board of County Commissioners unanimously adopted the 2025 Wildfire Resiliency code with Larimer County Amendments on September 22, 2025.
source_label: Larimer County Building, Building Codes (2025 Wildfire Resiliency Code, adopted September 22, 2025)
notes: larimer.gov returns 403 to curl. The live page was read through a fetch tool on 2026-09-25 (same adoption sentence) and word for word in the Wayback capture of 2026-03-07 (web.archive.org/web/20260307144840/https://www.larimer.gov/building/building/codes). The code applies to unincorporated Larimer County only; cities and towns adopt their own.

fact: Larimer County's amended Wildfire Resiliency Code deems all of unincorporated Larimer County a wildland-urban interface area, where structures and parcels must meet its structure-hardening and site requirements.
quote: Because of the history of and potential for large, destructive wildland fires, all of unincorporated Larimer County is deemed a wildland-urban interface area. Structures and parcels shall be constructed and maintained in accordance with the provisions for structure hardening of Chapter 4 and site and area requirements of Chapter 5.
source_label: Colorado Wildfire Resiliency Code as adopted by Larimer County, Sec. 302.1 as amended (recorded September 23, 2025)
notes: The PDF returns 403 to curl; fetched through a fetch tool on 2026-09-25 and read with pdftotext, checked against the page image (strikethrough text excluded). The state text this replaces left the interface areas to be declared from findings of fact.

fact: Larimer County's amended Wildfire Resiliency Code calls the first 5 feet around a structure the Immediate Zone, meant to reduce or eliminate ember ignition and direct flame contact, requires noncombustible, hard surface materials there such as rock, gravel, sand, concrete, bare earth or stone or concrete pavers, and requires plantings, combustible mulch and woody debris removed; the county struck the state code's exception for ignition-resistant plantings in that zone.
quote: 502.1 Structure Ignition Zone 1 (0-5 feet): Immediate Zone 502.1.1 Objective. This zone is designed to reduce or eliminate ember ignition and direct flame contact with the structure, decks, stairs, and attachments. … 502.1.2 Materials. Use noncombustible, hard surface materials in this zone, such as rock, gravel, sand, concrete, bare earth or stone/concrete pavers. … 502.1.3 Plantings. Remove all plantings including shrubs, slash, combustible mulch and other woody debris
source_label: Colorado Wildfire Resiliency Code as adopted by Larimer County, Sec. 502.1 as amended (effective January 1, 2026)
notes: Read with pdftotext and checked against the page image on 2026-09-25. Struck through in the county's copy: 'CLASS 1' in the Section 502 heading, the 502.1.2 exception ('Ignition resistant plantings, per an approved list by the AHJ … are allowed in the Immediate Zone') and ', with the exception of ignition resistant vegetation' in 502.1.3. Artificial turf is not named anywhere in the adopted text (searched); whether it may sit in the zone is the county's call, and the page says ask.

fact: The county's code defines a noncombustible building material as one of which no part will ignite and burn when subjected to fire, or any material conforming to ASTM E136.
quote: NONCOMBUSTIBLE. As applied to building construction material means a material that, in the form in which it is used, is either one of the following: 1. Material of which no part will ignite and burn when subjected to fire. 2. Any material conforming to ASTM E136 shall be considered noncombustible within the meaning of this section.
source_label: Colorado Wildfire Resiliency Code as adopted by Larimer County, Sec. 202, Definitions: Noncombustible
notes: Read with pdftotext on 2026-09-25. A third item (fire-rated gypsum board) follows and is not quoted.

fact: The county's code applies to the construction, alteration, movement, repair, maintenance and use of any building, structure or premises with occupiable or habitable space in the wildland-urban interface, and lets buildings or conditions that were legal when it was adopted continue unless they are a distinct danger to life or property.
quote: The provisions of this code shall apply to the construction, alteration, movement, repair, maintenance and use of any building, structure or premises that contain occupiable and/or habitable space, or change in use resulting in an occupiable and/or habitable space, unless excepted, within the wildland-urban interface areas of Colorado, as designated in this code. Buildings or conditions in existence at the time of the adoption of this code are allowed to have their use or occupancy continued, if such condition, use or occupancy was legal at the time of the adoption of this code, provided that such continued use does not constitute a distinct danger to life or property.
source_label: Colorado Wildfire Resiliency Code as adopted by Larimer County, Sec. 101.2, Scope
notes: Read with pdftotext and the page image on 2026-09-25. Sec. 101.4 adds that the code applies to conditions arising after its adoption; Sec. 101.7 brings the 5-foot immediate zone into compliance when 25 percent or more of an existing home's exterior walls are replaced. How the county applies these to a turf project on an existing lot is not stated; the page says ask.

fact: Berthoud's Landscape Design Guidelines say Berthoud is included in the Front Range wildland-urban interface, encourage owners to protect their property from wildfire, and list defensible space zones starting with an ember-resistant zone 0 to 5 feet from buildings and structures.
quote: The Wildland Urban Interface (WUI) is the area where homes and the urban environment press against the wildland. Berthoud is included in the WUI for the Front Range of Colorado. Property owners are encouraged to protect their property and their community from wildfire. … 5. Establish defensible space zones around structures … Zone 1 - Ember resistant zone (0-5 feet away from building and structures)
source_label: Town of Berthoud Landscape Design Guidelines, Emergency Planning: Wildland Urban Interface, p. 21 (updated June 30, 2026, Ordinance 1383)
notes: PDF read with pdftotext on 2026-09-25. Guidance ('encouraged', 'establish'), adopted by reference for new construction and substantial alterations reviewed by the town (berthoud-co.ldg-artificial-turf-backyards). It does not name artificial turf in the zone.

fact: Colorado's protection for backyard turf and water-wise landscaping at a detached home does not stop an HOA from adopting bona fide safety requirements consistent with landscape codes or recognized safety standards, or from prohibiting or restricting changes that interfere with fire buffers or defensible spaces.
quote: (V) NOTHING IN THIS SUBSECTION (1)(i.5) SHALL BE CONSTRUED TO PROHIBIT OR RESTRICT THE AUTHORITY OF ASSOCIATIONS TO: (A) ADOPT BONA FIDE SAFETY REQUIREMENTS CONSISTENT WITH APPLICABLE LANDSCAPE CODES OR RECOGNIZED SAFETY STANDARDS FOR THE PROTECTION OF PERSONS AND PROPERTY; (B) PROHIBIT OR RESTRICT CHANGES THAT INTERFERE WITH THE ESTABLISHMENT AND MAINTENANCE OF FIRE BUFFERS OR DEFENSIBLE SPACES; OR
notes: Read in the signed act with pdftotext on 2026-09-25 (page 3). Not legal advice. The backyard-turf protection itself is co-hoa-backyard-detached.
